items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: David Baker was there and he is a few years older than me but he’s like my big brother and he’s always looked out for me. In fact when I went to Yale University we were roommates.

ctx.x: Was jazz, before this seeing Ray Brown, was jazz part of your household?

Oh yes. My parents were into Duke Ellington, Count Basie. My mother’s youngest brother was into the more current stuff like with the bebop and stuff like that. And all these musicians around town, you know, like were all very supportive. There are so many names I hesitate to name a lot of names, but I mentioned the main ones like the Montgomery brothers and David Baker. David Baker was there and he is a few years older than me but he’s like my big brother and he’s always looked out for me. In fact when I went to…
Can you imagine that any of them could envision where that led? You know this gathering here is astounding to me.

items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He played with the big band that I had in 1958 and ’59.

ctx.x: Larry Ridley I met when Larry was in his teens. I convinced Larry, and a little earlier, David Young and George Bright, to come to Indiana University. I remember his mother, whom I saw at the Indy Jazz Fest – [I convinced her] to let Larry come to

school here – she let him come to school with the stipulation that I was going to be basically his on-campus guardian. First mistake. Larry came down here as a violinist. He was playing violin in the orchestra and gradually realized he wanted to play jazz. He was a contemporary of Jack Wilson, the piano player, [and] of Joe Hunt. Larry became an accomplished player. He played with the big band that I had in 1958 and ’59. That’s the band that included, like I said, Freddie Hubbard, Al Kiger, Joe Hunt, Lanny…
